name: Dhampus
tagline: A Gurung ridge village and the gentle start of Annapurna treks
meta_description: Dhampus near Pokhara: a Gurung ridge village at 1,650 m with Annapurna views, Australian Camp, the Mardi Himal trailhead, homestays and how to get there.
summary: Dhampus is a Gurung village spread along a ridge at about 1,650 m, an hour's drive northwest of Pokhara. It faces Annapurna South, Machhapuchhre and Dhaulagiri across the Modi valley, sits at the start of the Mardi Himal trek, and makes an easy one or two-night village stay from Pokhara.
intro: Dhampus is where many first-time trekkers feel the mountains come close. From Phedi, on the Pokhara–Baglung road, a stone staircase climbs about 500 m through forest and terraces to the long ridge where Dhampus's houses spread out over a few kilometres. Turn round at the top and Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre stand directly across the valley, with Dhaulagiri far to the west. The climb takes about two hours, and every step of it is used daily by villagers carrying loads.

The village is Gurung at its core, with stone houses, slate and tin roofs, millet terraces and buffalo sheds, and newer lodges built for trekkers along the trail. It lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so permits are checked here. From Dhampus the trail continues to Pothana and Australian Camp, then on to Mardi Himal, Landruk and the Annapurna Sanctuary. Lodges along the ridge have terraces facing the mountains, and the older houses sit just below them.

Most people pass through in an hour on day one of a trek. Stop instead. Spend a night, walk the ridge at sunset, eat with a family and watch the range turn pink at dawn without having climbed above 2,000 m. Families with young children and older travellers often find Dhampus and Australian Camp give them the Annapurna experience without a long trek. Altitude is not a concern at this height, though nights are cool.

story.title: A Gurung ridge on the Mardi trail
paras: Dhampus grew as a farming village on a sunny ridge above the Modi and Seti valleys, with water from springs and forests for fodder above. Gurung families, who call themselves Tamu, farmed millet, maize and rice on terraces carved down both sides, and sent their sons to the Gurkha regiments. The pension money, and later remittances from the Gulf and Malaysia, rebuilt many houses. Many households also kept bees, buffalo and goats, and some still do.

For decades Dhampus was a stop on the trail between Pokhara's valley and the villages of the Modi Khola, and later on early treks into the Annapurna Sanctuary. At the 1991 census about 2,750 people lived in its 547 households. As trekking grew, families opened tea houses along the path, and the area joined the Annapurna Conservation Area, which shapes how the forest is used and how lodges operate. Lodge owners agreed standards and prices through local committees.

The opening of the Mardi Himal route to teahouse trekking in the 2010s brought Dhampus a new role as a trailhead. A road now reaches the village, so jeeps can drop walkers at the top of the steps. The farms and the Gurung festivals continue alongside: Tamu Lhosar at the end of December, harvest work in October, and weddings in the cool months when soldiers come home on leave. Farming still sets the rhythm of the year.

people: Dhampus is mainly Gurung, with Brahmin, Chhetri and Dalit households in parts of the village. Most families farm and keep buffalo and goats, and many have members in the British or Indian Gurkhas, in Gulf countries or in Pokhara. Gurung religious life mixes Buddhist lamas with the older Pachyu and Ghyabri priests, who perform funeral and household rites. Lodge-keeping is now a major income on the trail.

untold.fact: At the 1991 census Dhampus village development committee had 2,753 people in 547 households; it lies on the Mardi Himal trekking route and is close to Australian Camp, with views of Annapurna, Dhaulagiri and Machhapuchhre.

Gurung religious life has two kinds of traditional priests besides Buddhist lamas: the Pachyu (Paju) and the Ghyabri (Ghyabring), who perform rites such as funerals, and some villages keep traces of pre-Buddhist Bon practice.
The Gurung call themselves Tamu and their language Tamu Kyi, a tonal Tibeto-Burman language of the Tamangic group, related to Thakali and Manange.

taste.name: Kodo ko roti with honey
taste.text: Flat bread of finger millet flour, dark and nutty, cooked on a griddle and eaten with local honey, ghee or a pickle. Gurung kitchens in Dhampus make it for breakfast, and some lodges serve it if asked the evening before. Millet is the old staple of these ridges.

facts: Gurung village, Annapurna views, Mardi Himal trailhead

highlights.title: Annapurna South across the valley
highlights.text: From the ridge Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre fill the view to the north, with Dhaulagiri to the west. Sunset and sunrise light are best from October to February. Ask for a north-facing room or terrace for the best view.

highlights.title: The steps from Phedi
highlights.text: A stone staircase and forest path climb about 500 m from Phedi on the Baglung road to Dhampus in around two hours, the classic first climb of many Annapurna treks. Walking poles help on the steep stone steps.

highlights.title: Australian Camp
highlights.text: A grassy clearing at about 2,060 m, an easy walk from Dhampus via Pothana, with wide mountain views and a few lodges. Popular for a first night out of Pokhara. Families with children often walk here and back in two days.

highlights.title: Gurung village life
highlights.text: Walk the ridge path past stone houses, millet terraces and buffalo sheds. Evenings bring families home from the fields and children practising for school exams by headlamp. A local guide can introduce you to families and explain what you see.

highlights.title: Start of the Mardi Himal trek
highlights.text: The Mardi Himal route climbs from here through Pothana and Forest Camp to the ridge under Machhapuchhre, making Dhampus the natural first night. The first day from Dhampus to Forest Camp is long and climbs through dense forest.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Pokhara to Phedi on the Pokhara–Baglung road, about 20 km and 40–50 minutes, then either walk up or continue on the road to Dhampus by jeep, around 30–45 minutes more. Local buses for Baglung stop at Phedi. A private jeep from Lakeside is easiest.

From Phedi (about 1,130 m) a stone staircase climbs to Dhampus in 1.5–2 hours. From Dhampus, Pothana and Australian Camp are 1.5–2.5 hours further, and the trail continues to Mardi Himal or down to Landruk and the Modi Khola.

where_to_stay: Dhampus has a string of family lodges and homestays along the ridge, with simple rooms, shared or attached bathrooms and big terraces facing the Annapurnas. Australian Camp and Pothana, an hour or two further, have similar lodges. Expect hot showers powered by solar or gas, dal bhat and a few Western dishes. There are no luxury hotels; for comfort, sleep in Pokhara at Temple Tree Resort or Hotel Barahi and come up for the day.
tips: Dhampus is inside the Annapurna Conservation Area: carry your ACAP permit and TIMS card, and walk with a licensed guide; check current status before you travel.
Climb the Phedi steps in the morning or late afternoon; midday is hot below 1,500 m in spring.
Ask for a north-facing room, the views are the reason to sleep here.
Lodge Wi-Fi and phone signal are usually available but can drop in bad weather.
Carry cash; few lodges take cards and the nearest ATMs are in Pokhara.

experiences.title: Climb the Phedi steps to Dhampus
experiences.summary: The classic first climb of Annapurna trekking: about 500 m of stone steps and forest path from Phedi on the Baglung road up to the Dhampus ridge, with the snow peaks appearing at the top.
body: Phedi means the foot of a hill, and that is what it is: a handful of shops on the Pokhara–Baglung road where the trail begins. You cross a small stream and start up. The steps are uneven stone, laid by villagers and maintained over decades, climbing steeply through forest of chestnut, schima and rhododendron with glimpses of terraces through the trees. Some sections are steep enough that you will want to stop every few minutes, and that is fine.

Go slowly. Your guide will say bistarai, slowly, and mean it. You share the path with villagers carrying loads, schoolchildren running down and porters heading up. Tea shops appear at the right moments. After about an hour and a half the gradient eases, the trees open and the first houses of Dhampus appear. Children may walk with you for a while and practise their English; it is a friendly trail.

Then the reward: from the ridge, Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre stand across the valley, often with the morning still clear. Stop for tea on a lodge terrace and let your legs recover. Many walkers decide here that they like trekking; a few decide they will take the jeep next time. If you arrive in the morning, the views are usually clear until about 10 am. Lodges serve lunch from late morning, and many walkers continue to Pothana or Australian Camp in the afternoon.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Phedi to Dhampus?
faqs.a: Most walkers take 1.5–2 hours from Phedi to the first houses of Dhampus, climbing about 500 m on stone steps and forest path. Fit walkers do it faster, families with children slower. Coming down takes about an hour. The village is long, so allow extra time to reach lodges further along the ridge.

faqs.q: Can I drive to Dhampus instead of walking?
faqs.a: Yes. A road now reaches Dhampus from the Baglung road, and jeeps from Pokhara take about 1.5 hours in total. It is useful for older travellers, young children or those with heavy bags. The road is rough in places and can be closed by mud in the monsoon. Walking up the steps is the traditional and more rewarding way.

faqs.q: Is the Phedi to Dhampus trail difficult?
faqs.a: It is steep but short. The whole climb is stone steps and path with no exposure, so the challenge is fitness and knees rather than skill. Walking poles help. Start early to avoid heat and take breaks at tea shops. Anyone who can climb stairs for an hour or two at a steady pace can manage it.

experiences.title: Walk to Australian Camp for sunset
experiences.summary: From Dhampus, walk through forest and Pothana to the grassy clearing of Australian Camp at about 2,060 m, watch the sun set on Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre, and sleep in a lodge on the meadow.
body: The trail from Dhampus climbs gently through mixed forest to Pothana, a small settlement of lodges, then on to Australian Camp. It is an easy half day with tea stops, rising about 400 m. Rhododendron trees line the trail and flower red from March. The path is wide and well marked, with occasional mule trains and porters carrying supplies to the lodges. Pothana's lodges make a good tea stop, and there is time to sit and watch the clouds on the peaks.

Australian Camp is an open grassy shelf at about 2,060 m, with lodges at its edge. The view is wide: Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Machhapuchhre and the Annapurna peaks to the east, with the Pokhara valley to the south on clear days. Families spread out on the grass, and guides play cards in the late sun. There is no village here, only lodges, so evenings are quiet. Order dinner early and take a warm layer outside for the stars.

Stay for sunset, when the snow turns gold and then pink, and again for sunrise, when the peaks come out of the dark one by one. From here you can return to Pokhara via Kande in about an hour's walk and a short drive, continue to Mardi Himal, or drop down to Landruk on the way to the Sanctuary. Nights are cold from November to February, so bring a warm sleeping bag or ask for extra blankets.

faqs.q: Why is it called Australian Camp?
faqs.a: The clearing has been called Australian Camp for decades, and the name is said to come from an Australian trekking group that camped here, though we have not found a firm record. Locals and signposts use the name. It is a grassy shelf at about 2,060 m with lodges and wide views of Annapurna South, Machhapuchhre and the Annapurna range.

faqs.q: How far is Australian Camp from Dhampus?
faqs.a: Australian Camp is about 1.5–2.5 hours' walk from Dhampus via Pothana, climbing gently around 400 m through forest. It can also be reached from Kande on the Baglung road in about an hour of steady climbing, which makes it one of the most accessible mountain viewpoints near Pokhara. Many families do a one-night round trip.

faqs.q: Is Australian Camp good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. The walk is short, the lodges are simple but comfortable, and the grassy clearing gives children space to play with a view of the Annapurnas. Nights are cold from November to February, so bring warm layers. The altitude of about 2,060 m poses no problem for healthy children. An ACAP permit is needed.

experiences.title: Gurung village walk along the Dhampus ridge
experiences.summary: An unhurried walk through the older parts of Dhampus with a local guide: stone houses, millet terraces, water taps and shrines, with conversation about Gurung life, the Gurkhas and how the village has changed with the trekking trail.
body: Most trekkers see only the line of lodges along the trail. The older village lies off it, on paths between stone houses with carved window frames, stacked firewood and courtyards where grain dries on woven mats. Walk it in the late afternoon, when people come back from the fields and the light softens. The houses are spread out along the ridge, so a walk of an hour or two covers several clusters and shows how the village is organised around water sources and fields.

Your guide can explain what you are seeing: the family shrine, the communal water tap where news is exchanged, the terraces of kodo millet that once fed the village, and the houses rebuilt with army pensions. Many families have a photograph of a father or grandfather in Gurkha uniform. If invited in, remove shoes and accept tea; it is polite to drink at least a little. Tea will often be milky and sweet, served with beaten rice or roasted corn.

Ask about Gurung customs: Tamu Lhosar at the end of December, the Pachyu and Ghyabri priests who perform funeral rites, the rodhi tradition of young people meeting to sing and work together. Be respectful with the camera, ask before photographing people, and do not hand out sweets to children. Offering a small donation to a school or community fund through your guide is a better way to help. If you are lucky, you may hear older women singing as they work or see preparations for a wedding or festival.

faqs.q: Who are the Gurung people?
faqs.a: The Gurung, who call themselves Tamu, are a Tibeto-Burman speaking people of the hills of Gandaki Province, including Kaski, Lamjung, Syangja, Manang and Gorkha. Their language is Tamu Kyi. Many are farmers and many have served in the British, Indian and other armies as Gurkhas. Their religion mixes Buddhism with older Pachyu and Ghyabri traditions.

faqs.q: Is it okay to photograph people in Dhampus?
faqs.a: Ask first, with a smile and a gesture, and respect a no. Elders and children are often happy to be photographed, but people working or praying may not be. Do not photograph inside homes or shrines without permission. Showing people the photo on your screen is appreciated. Avoid paying for photos, which changes how villagers see visitors.

faqs.q: Can I visit a Gurung home in Dhampus?
faqs.a: Yes, homestays and some lodges are family homes, and a local guide can introduce you to families who welcome visitors. Remove shoes at the door, accept tea, avoid stepping over the fire or pointing feet at people, and use your right hand to give or take. A small gift of fruit or school supplies is welcome but not expected.

experiences.title: Cook dal bhat and millet roti with a Gurung family
experiences.summary: Join a Dhampus family in the kitchen to cook the evening meal: dal, rice, seasonal vegetables, pickles and millet roti, cooked on a wood or gas fire and eaten together. A homestay highlight, arranged in advance.
body: Dinner in a hill village starts long before dark. Rice is picked over, lentils soaked, greens picked from the garden. Your host will show you how to temper dal with jimbu or cumin in hot ghee, how to fry saag with garlic and chilli, and how to grind a tomato and timur pickle on a flat stone. The fire is the centre of the house. Kitchens are smoky and low, so keep your head down and your camera away from the fire.

Millet is the old grain of these ridges. Kodo flour becomes thick dhido, stirred hard in a heavy pot, or flat roti cooked on a griddle. Taste them with ghee and you understand why older villagers still prefer them to rice. In season there may be gundruk, fermented dried greens, or a local chicken curry for guests. Honey from local hives is sometimes served with breakfast roti.

Eat together, usually sitting near the fire. Use your right hand if you want to eat Nepali style, or ask for a spoon. Second and third servings will be offered; to stop, say pugyo, enough, and cover the plate with your hand. Arrange the cooking session through your guide a day ahead. Tell your host about any allergies or diet needs; vegetarian food is normal and easy. A small payment for the experience is usually included in the homestay price.

faqs.q: Can I take a cooking class in Dhampus?
faqs.a: There is no formal cooking school, but homestays and family lodges in Dhampus will often let you join the kitchen and cook the evening meal with them if you ask in advance. Your guide can arrange it. Expect a relaxed, hands-on session rather than a structured class, and a meal of dal bhat and seasonal vegetables.

faqs.q: What is dhido?
faqs.a: Dhido is a thick, smooth porridge made by stirring millet, buckwheat or maize flour into boiling water until it becomes stiff. It is eaten with dal, greens, pickle and ghee, by hand, and was the staple of hill villages before rice became common. It is filling and slow-burning, ideal for trekking days.

faqs.q: Is homestay food safe for travellers?
faqs.a: Freshly cooked, hot food from a family kitchen is generally safe. Drink boiled, filtered or treated water, avoid raw salads if you have a sensitive stomach, and wash or sanitise your hands before eating. Tell your host about allergies, vegetarian or other needs in advance; vegetarian dal bhat is normal and easy to provide.

faqs.q: How do I get to Dhampus from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Drive about 20 km on the Pokhara–Baglung road to Phedi, 40–50 minutes, then walk up the stone steps in 1.5–2 hours. Alternatively, a jeep can drive all the way to Dhampus, about 1.5 hours from Pokhara. Local Baglung buses stop at Phedi. Most trekkers use a private jeep booked through their agency or hotel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Dhampus?
faqs.a: Dhampus village sits at about 1,650 m on a ridge, roughly 500 m above Phedi and 800 m above Pokhara. Australian Camp nearby is about 2,060 m. These heights pose no altitude risk for healthy visitors. Nights are cool, especially from November to February, when lodges supply blankets and you will want a warm jacket.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Dhampus?
faqs.a: Yes. Dhampus is inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so you need an ACAP permit and a TIMS card, and since April 2023 foreign trekkers must walk with a licensed guide. Permits are checked on the trail. They are issued in Kathmandu and Pokhara. Rules have changed several times, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Dhampus worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you want mountain views and village life without a long trek. From the ridge, Annapurna South, Machhapuchhre and Dhaulagiri are in full view, and the Gurung village is friendly and lived-in. It suits families, older travellers and short trips, and it is the natural first night of the Mardi Himal trek.

faqs.q: Can you see Machhapuchhre from Dhampus?
faqs.a: Yes. Machhapuchhre is one of the main peaks in view, along with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Annapurna II to IV to the east and Dhaulagiri far to the west. Its fishtail shape is less obvious from this angle than from Pokhara. Views are clearest at sunrise and sunset from October to February.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Dhampus?
faqs.a: One night is enough to see sunset and sunrise and walk the village. Two nights let you add Australian Camp or a longer walk. Many people visit as the first night of a Mardi Himal or Annapurna Base Camp trek. A combined Dhampus and Australian Camp loop from Pokhara takes two nights at an easy pace.

faqs.q: What are the lodges like in Dhampus?
faqs.a: Simple family lodges and homestays, with twin rooms, blankets, shared or attached bathrooms and solar or gas hot showers. Dining rooms serve dal bhat, noodles, momo and some Western dishes. Terraces face the Annapurnas. There are no luxury hotels. Wi-Fi is usually available but slow. Bring a sleeping bag liner and headlamp.

faqs.q: Is Dhampus suitable for elderly travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, by jeep. The road now reaches the village, so you can avoid the steep climb from Phedi and still enjoy the views and village walks. Lodges are simple, with steps between levels and sometimes outside bathrooms, so check rooms in advance. Altitude is not an issue at 1,650 m.

faqs.q: What is the best season to visit Dhampus?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest mountain views and dry trails. February to April are warm with rhododendrons in flower on the way to Australian Camp, though afternoon haze builds. December and January are clear but cold at night. June to September brings monsoon rain, cloud, mud and leeches, and we do not recommend it.
